opus-5.5.text:
Well, I came to it as a physicist, and I think that shaped what I was looking for. When I arrived, a lot of the work was very descriptive: careful modeling of particular circuits, particular neurons, a particular experimental setup, and fitting models with many parameters to reproduce what was observed. That's valuable, but I kept asking myself what general principle I'd learned at the end. Often it was hard to say.

The deeper problem, for me, was that the central question of intelligence is *learning*: how a system with very limited data manages to extract structure from a very high-dimensional world. That's the curse of dimensionality. If you think naively about learning a generic function in, say, a thousand dimensions, the number of examples you'd need is astronomical. Yet brains, and now artificial networks, learn from relatively few examples. So the world must have some structure, and the learning system must be exploiting it. To me that was *the* question, and I didn't feel the neuroscience I was seeing had the tools, or even the framing, to attack it. Biology is enormously complicated, and you can't easily do controlled experiments where you vary the data, the architecture, the training procedure, and see what happens.

So when deep learning started working spectacularly, I saw an opportunity. Here was a system that genuinely learns, which you can open up completely, measure anything in, and perturb at will. It's almost like a model organism for intelligence, but one where you have full experimental access. And as a physicist, that's a dream: you can look for phenomena, scaling laws, phase transitions, and try to build minimal models that explain them. The questions become sharper: What is the structure of data, like images or text, that makes it learnable? How do networks build hierarchical representations that become invariant to irrelevant transformations? Why does performance improve as a power law with the amount of data?

Those felt like questions where you could actually make progress and get general answers, rather than describing one system in great detail without knowing what carries over. That's really what pushed me away from theoretical neuroscience as I'd encountered it, and toward the theory of deep learning.

r001.rationale: He says the neuroscience he encountered focused on detailed circuit and neuron models but lacked the tools or framing to address the central question of how systems learn intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say first that I came to neuroscience as a physicist. My training was in statistical physics, so I was used to a certain way of thinking: you have a system with many degrees of freedom, and you look for the small number of quantities that actually control its behavior. You look for universality. And when I went into theoretical neuroscience as a postdoc, I found a field that was, in a sense, full of very beautiful models, but very hard to connect to the question I actually cared about, which is: why does learning work at all?

The difficulty was really at two levels. The first is that the brain is an extraordinarily complicated object, and the data at the time was very partial. You could record a few neurons, maybe a few hundred, and build models of how a particular circuit might implement a particular computation. These models could be quite elegant. But you never had the feeling that you could test the model in a decisive way, because there was always a lot of freedom in the assumptions you had to make. The models were underconstrained. In physics, you want a situation where the theory makes a sharp prediction and the experiment can kill it. That loop was very weak.

The second level, which I think is deeper, is that even if you had a perfect description of some circuit, it was not clear it would tell you anything general about intelligence. Many of the models were about a specific task, a specific area, a specific animal. There was not really a framework for asking the question I found most interesting: what makes a problem learnable? Why can a system with a finite amount of data generalize to situations it has never seen? That is a question about the structure of the data and the structure of the learning algorithm, and it is largely independent of whether the substrate is biological or not.

So I had this somewhat frustrating experience where I felt the field was asking the right questions in spirit but did not have the tools to answer them. And then, a bit later, deep learning arrived, and suddenly you had a system where you could do the experiment. You control the architecture, you control the data, you can vary the dimension, the number of samples, the depth, everything. And these systems display phenomena that look very much like phase transitions, like scaling laws, things a statistical physicist recognizes immediately. So for me it was a bit like going back to what I knew how to do, but now with an object that was genuinely learning. That is why I moved in that direction: not because the brain is uninteresting, but because neural networks were the first learning systems where I felt a theory could actually be built and tested.

r001.rationale: The response says the neuroscience models were hard to connect to why learning works and did not provide a general framework for explaining intelligence or generalization.

astra-6.text:
What I found unsatisfying was the gap between the questions we could address and the questions that interested me. In theoretical neuroscience, you could study a network of neurons and characterize its dynamics—whether its activity was stable, irregular, or synchronized. Those are interesting problems, and they are quite natural for a physicist. But understanding the dynamics of a network doesn't, by itself, explain how it learns something useful or how it generalizes to a new situation.

I wanted to understand intelligence at that level: what makes learning possible, and what determines whether it succeeds? I didn't see a clear route from the models I was encountering to those questions. That's not to say that the biological details are unimportant. It was more that I was missing a framework connecting those details to an actual ability to learn.

r001.rationale: The response says studying network dynamics did not explain how a network learns something useful, and that Wyart saw no clear route from those models to understanding learning.

sol-6.1.text:
What I found unsatisfying was the gap between describing the activity of neurons and understanding what computation that activity achieves. You could study a network, characterize its dynamics, and find interesting collective behavior. But it was often unclear how that helped explain an animal learning something or solving a problem.

For me, the question was: what makes learning possible, and what determines how difficult it is? You need a task, some notion of performance, and a way to connect the properties of the network to that performance. Otherwise, you can have a very sophisticated model of neural activity without really getting closer to understanding intelligence.

That’s what attracted me to studying learning more directly. It gives you a setting where you can ask precise questions about what a system learns and why it succeeds or fails.

r001.rationale: The candidate says neuronal dynamics did not explain what computation the activity achieved or how an animal learned or solved problems, conveying the disconnect from explaining intelligence through learning.
